note: Covers fourteen sectors with barriers named, useful for scoping an audit at a diversified client.
title: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in Business: A Systematic Review on the Threshold of Transformation

reading.body:
A 2024 systematic review maps generative AI benefits, risks, and adoption barriers across fourteen named sectors, and its central claim is that adoption speed, not capability, decides who absorbs the disruption.

The pattern is breadth without depth. Fourteen sectors are covered, and the barriers are named rather than measured: privacy exposure, biased outputs, and regulatory uncertainty recur across them. The model families listed, GANs, transformers, VAEs, and diffusion models, are matched to industry needs in principle, but the review synthesizes existing studies rather than producing new deployment evidence. Twenty-eight citations is a modest base for a claim this wide.

For AI specifically, the useful part is the framing of delay as the risk. The review argues that slow adoption brings workforce disruption and ethical problems, which inverts the usual caution. That matters because it treats integration work, technical foundations, employee training, and ethical oversight as prerequisites rather than afterthoughts. Those are organizational costs, and they land before any compute is bought.

What the data does not cover is the physical side. There is no discussion of data centers, power, or hardware anywhere in the record, so nothing here speaks to whether these fourteen sectors can actually get the compute their use cases imply. The review also gives no sector-level numbers, no adoption rates, and no cost figures. It is a scoping document, useful for naming what to audit at a diversified client, not for sizing what the answer will cost.

explain_beginner: This paper reviews how generative AI can affect many areas, from health and education to farming and online shopping. It says these tools can speed up work, improve decisions, and use resources better. But it also warns that waiting too long can cause job losses and hard moral questions. The authors point to problems like keeping personal information safe, unfair results, and unclear rules. They suggest preparing technology, training workers, and using strong ethical oversight. The main message is that organizations should adopt these tools carefully to stay competitive and helpful to society.
explain_business: This review suggests generative AI can improve efficiency, spark new ideas, and support faster choices in many industries. It warns that slow adoption may bring workforce disruption and ethical problems, while privacy, bias, and regulation remain major hurdles. For executives, the practical takeaway is to assess where these tools fit, strengthen technical foundations, train people, and set clear ethical controls. The paper also stresses that adoption is urgent for remaining competitive and viable over time. It recommends working across sectors and shaping flexible policies so innovation stays aligned with social values.
explain_practitioner: This review of existing studies surveys generative AI uses across fourteen sectors and sorts benefits, risks, and adoption barriers. It reports gains such as automating difficult workflows, improving resource allocation, and making decisions faster. It also names obstacles including privacy worries, biased algorithms, and regulatory uncertainty. The paper discusses practical integration steps: prepared technical foundations, training employees, and ethical oversight. It covers model families such as GANs, Transformer based systems, VAEs, and diffusion models, noting they can be matched to industry needs. The key result is a synthesized view that responsible deployment requires balancing innovation with risk reduction and cooperation across industries.
